bundles.changelog: First concrete foundation-bundle prerelease package (six foundation-document templates with their own schema and hash baselines).
Reworks the technical-architecture document so cross-cutting content lives in one place and is cross-referenced rather than duplicated.
Your built system can now APPLY foundation-document upgrades (not just detect them); upgrades became repeatable, quieter, and clearer, and merge your edits with the new version where possible.
You now build and run your system one capability at a time, accepting each before building the next (the build-and-operate loop with per-phase acceptance).
bundles.recommendation_reason: You now build and run your system one capability at a time, accepting each before the next.

bundles.changelog: Your system now keeps you oriented and protects risky actions; can receive operating-layer improvements through an upgrade (not just foundation documents); and can check for and safely apply its own updates.
bundles.recommendation_reason: Adds operator orientation and risk-action protections, and lets your system safely apply its own updates.

bundles.changelog: The approval drill (the one-time safety demonstration) now uses an example grounded in what your system actually does, instead of a generic action.
bundles.recommendation_reason: The approval drill now uses an example grounded in what your system actually does.

bundles.changelog: Updating your system is now one safe step: the assistant refreshes the update tool and applies the update together. Also hardens two safety details — the record of an approved update can no longer be altered, and the start-of-session update check uses the same trusted source as the manual check.
bundles.recommendation_reason: Makes updating your system one safe step and hardens two update-safety details.

bundles.changelog: Fixes a safety-check bug that was stopping you to approve ordinary edits to your own notes and documents — everyday words like "firm" or "High" were mistaken for risky commands, which both broke auto mode and trained you to click through every prompt. The check now decides by what an action actually does, so it pauses only for genuinely risky, irreversible, or outgoing actions. Also adds a short note explaining why auto mode still pauses before sending, sharing, or deleting.
bundles.recommendation_reason: Fixes a safety-check bug that was interrupting your ordinary edits and training you to click through every prompt.

bundles.changelog: Fixes the update flow so your system no longer talks you out of safe updates. When you ask "what's new?", it now runs the update check and reports exactly what the check found — a plain-language summary, the system's own recommendation, and the one command to apply it — instead of a vague walkthrough. A version being labeled prerelease or missing detailed notes is never treated as a reason to wait, and if your update tool is behind, the check routes you straight to the one-step refresh-and-apply.
bundles.recommendation_reason: Stops your system from talking you out of safe updates — the update check now reports a clear recommendation and never treats a normal prerelease label or missing notes as a reason to wait.

bundles.changelog: Improves how updates are previewed and applied. When an update is available, your system now runs a read-only preview that shows exactly what would change -- and that preview works even when the update tool is behind, so it can never wrongly tell you there is 'nothing to show'. You then approve, and the apply installs exactly the version you previewed (if the official source moved in between, it stops and re-previews rather than installing something different). The apply command is also kept short so it can't break when pasted.
bundles.recommendation_reason: Makes updates safer to approve: your system now shows you a read-only preview of exactly what an update changes before anything is applied, and the apply installs exactly what you previewed.

bundles.changelog: Smooths out the update experience. When an update is available your system keeps offering the full set of choices -- see what's new, remind me later, skip this version, or not now -- even if you've asked it to lead with a single next step; remind-later and skip are remembered so the reminder actually pauses. And once you approve an update, the assistant runs the update commands for you (resolving the tool's location so they can't fail with 'command not found') rather than asking you to paste them into a terminal.
bundles.recommendation_reason: Makes updating smoother: your system keeps offering the remind-later / skip / not-now choices for an update, and once you approve it runs the update for you instead of asking you to type a command.

bundles.changelog: Simplifies and makes consistent how updates are checked and applied. Your system now uses one clear path -- it checks (which reports what's new and its recommendation), and once you approve, the assistant applies the update for you. A separate preview step that the system's own instructions did not actually use has been removed, so the update flow behaves the same way every time.
bundles.recommendation_reason: A small consistency fix to the update process -- your system now follows one clear path to check for and apply updates.

bundles.changelog: Makes the update process more reliable. When the system checks for or applies an update, it now always runs the update tool by its full path instead of a short name that was sometimes not recognized -- so the update step no longer trips over a 'command not found' message. Nothing about your data or what updates do has changed.
bundles.recommendation_reason: A small reliability fix to the update process -- update commands now always use the tool's full path, so checking for and applying updates never fails with a 'command not found' message.

bundles.changelog: Your system now produces outputs in a consistent, predictable location (a deliverables/ folder with a clear naming convention established at setup). It also ships maintained output-quality guidance — channel-appropriate formatting for email and SMS, clearer message organization — that your agents consult when producing anything you will read or send. A design-pass skill runs before significant outbound messages to check rendering and organization against your preferences before anything is sent.
bundles.recommendation_reason: Your system now knows where to put its outputs and how to format them for the right channel — outputs land in a predictable place, and significant messages get a design pass before they go out.

bundles.changelog: Adds write-integrity protection for systems that send data back out to an external destination (a spreadsheet, a tracker, an outside service). Writes now go through a checked path: each value is validated against the set of values you allow before it leaves, significant writes are proposed to you in plain language and recorded with your approval, and a build-time check flags any write that tries to bypass the safe path. Each agent's permitted write destinations are derived and shown in a single audit table. Systems that do not write back to anything carry none of this — it is added only where it is needed. Your own data, rules, credentials, and logs are untouched.
bundles.recommendation_reason: When your system writes back to an outside destination, it now does so through a checked path — values are validated against your allowed set, significant writes get a fresh plain-language approval, and a build-time check flags anything that tries to go around the safe path.

bundles.changelog: Changes your system makes to data outside itself now carry an integrity contract: success is confirmed through an independent route (never by re-reading its own write), new write logic is proven on a copy before first live use, and undo is proven to restore your data.
bundles.recommendation_reason: Adds an integrity contract for changes your system makes to data outside itself — independent verification, copy-first proof, and proven undo.

bundles.changelog: Adds the operator-originated-enhancement flow: when you ask for something outside the current plan, your system now defines it, builds it, and records your acceptance before it goes live — with a build-time coverage check and a runtime write gate that ensure every capability that writes outside your system is declared, risk-classified, and approved by you. Includes a new add-capability skill, a machine-readable record of your system's write-back capabilities and their acceptance state, and an always-on commit-hygiene guard that keeps a clean baseline before building and commits each accepted phase as its own revertable unit. Systems that never write outside themselves carry none of the write-gating. Your own data, rules, credentials, and logs are untouched.
bundles.recommendation_reason: Your system can now safely take on new capabilities you ask for mid-run — it defines, builds, and gets your acceptance before anything goes live.

bundles.changelog: When your system is trying out a new capability that changes things outside itself, it can now safely test it two new ways before you accept it — a small, capped batch on your real data (with a proven undo path), or a preview run that changes nothing at all. A capped limit and your per-item approval bound the small-batch test; the preview never writes anything.
bundles.recommendation_reason: Your system can now test a new capability that changes things outside itself before you accept it — on a small, capped slice of your real data with a proven undo path, or in a preview that changes nothing at all.

bundles.changelog: When you come back to your system — at the start of a session or after a pause — it now leads with the step you actually left off on (including a paused or half-finished task), instead of picking an unrelated item off a date list. And when it saves where things stand, it records only the version you are on right now, never a guess like "no update expected next time" that a later check could prove wrong.
bundles.recommendation_reason: When you come back to your system, it now leads with the step you actually left off on instead of an unrelated item off a date list, and it never records a guess about a future version check.

bundles.changelog: Two additions under the hood. An adapter registry enforces a cap on how many things a single write action can touch; a read-only view lets a capability be built and tested without the code that builds it ever being able to touch the credential that can write; and a clearer three-way split between the code your system trusts by default, the code a connected service's adapter runs, and the code a specific capability runs makes it easier to see what any given piece of code is and is not allowed to do. A Gmail adapter (label and filter actions only — never sending, never permanently deleting) proves these building blocks out as a second real capability. And when your system checks for and applies an update, it now also checks whether anything you already had running still follows the current safety rules — if something no longer does, that one thing is safely paused, reversibly, and handed to the same define → build → accept process you already use to add a new capability, rather than left running unprotected or broken outright. No breaking changes: everything your system could already do continues to work exactly as before, and every previously released version still installs and runs correctly.
bundles.recommendation_reason: Future writes-back capabilities get more proven building blocks, and if something you already had running no longer follows your system's current safety rules, an update now catches it and pauses it safely instead of breaking it.

bundles.changelog: One addition under the hood: a run-level safety envelope for bulk actions. When a capability acts on many things at once, a single running ledger now tracks everything that run touches, an overall ceiling caps how much one run can change (scaled to how reversible the action is, on top of the existing cap on a single action), and the run does exactly the set you reviewed — if the plan changed after you approved it, the run stops rather than acting on something you did not see. "Verified" now means the change was confirmed against your real account, both when a capability is proven and each time it runs, not just that the code finished. And the exact sentence you approve is built from what the run will really do, so what you consent to always matches what happens. No breaking changes: everything your system could already do continues to work exactly as before, and every previously released version still installs and runs correctly.
bundles.recommendation_reason: Bulk actions that change many things at once are now bounded and verified as a whole run: an overall ceiling caps a single run, the run does exactly what you reviewed, and "verified" means checked against your real account — so a large batch is safe to run and easy to trust.

bundles.changelog: Four additions under the hood. Getting a newly built capability approved and running is now turnkey — the operator-acceptance step no longer refuses a freshly built capability just because nothing had loaded its code yet. Deciding what belongs in a bulk approval now has its own tool: it groups and classifies candidates for you and binds your approval to exactly what you were shown, so a run can never quietly act on something you did not see. A recurring or unattended job (a filter sweep, a scheduled digest, ...) can no longer fall through to a real run on a flag it does not recognize — it always has a safe preview, and an unrecognized instruction stops it rather than running anyway. And a credential that needs a specific permission (an OAuth scope) is now checked for that exact permission before anything live is attempted, with an honest three-state record (not granted / granted but unproven / verified) — and if a permission is not ready yet, only the live trial for that one part is paused; everything else stays built and running. No breaking changes: everything your system could already do continues to work exactly as before, and every previously released version still installs and runs correctly.
bundles.recommendation_reason: If you build new write-back capabilities, approve batches of changes, run anything on a schedule, or use a credential that needs a specific permission, this update makes each of those safer and easier to trust — most operators should take it.

bundles.changelog: This update makes an upgrade safer around your capabilities. First, the safety check that runs during an update now also looks at a capability you added yourself (not just the ones your system shipped with) — so if one of those can no longer run (for example, because an earlier update retired something it depended on), the update catches it and will not invite you back into it; instead it tells you plainly what needs fixing before you resume. Second, applying an update now always requires your own separate, explicit "yes, apply it" — asking to see what is new, or getting a notice that an update is available, never applies anything by itself. Third, running an update keeps your system's scripts able to run afterward, on top of everything you already had. No breaking changes: everything your system could already do continues to work exactly as before, and every previously released version still installs and runs correctly.
bundles.recommendation_reason: If your system runs a capability you added yourself (not one it shipped with), this update makes sure an upgrade will not invite you back into one that has stopped working, and makes sure applying any future update always asks you first — most operators should take it.

bundles.changelog: Three additions under the hood, plus a deeper self-check before any new capability goes live. First, your system now checks that a capability's name, its file, and its internal record all agree with each other before it lets you approve, run, or trust it — so a capability that was accidentally set up under a mismatched name is caught before it can cause confusion, not after. Second, if a capability's own code changes — through a rebuild, or because an earlier update retired something it depended on — your system now recognizes that its prior approval no longer applies and asks you to re-approve it before it runs again, instead of quietly trusting an approval that no longer matches what the capability actually does. Third, building a new capability now runs an additional, deterministic self-check before its first live trial, catching a class of test-quality problems (tests that would not actually have caught a real mistake) before you ever see the capability run for real. No breaking changes: everything your system could already do continues to work exactly as before, and every previously released version still installs and runs correctly.
bundles.recommendation_reason: If you build new capabilities, or if you rebuild or update one you already have, this update makes sure your approval always matches what the capability currently does, and adds an extra check before a new capability's first live run — most operators should take it.

bundles.changelog: Five improvements to how your system handles a large batch of changes, tests a new capability, and keeps a record of what it did. If a big batch of writes gets interrupted, it now safely picks back up from exactly where it stopped, using the one approval you already gave — it will never restart from scratch, silently skip pieces, or ask you to approve the same batch again. Building a new capability now proves, as a standard check, that its own tests would actually catch a real mistake and do not depend on unrelated leftover state from an earlier run; approving a capability also tidies up any leftover internal marker, and a naming mix-up between something you've only described and something you've actually built is now caught and reported plainly. Finishing an approval that had a related pending task now also completes that task, and a capability an update safely paused can be brought back through the same guided build-and-approve flow used for a new one. You can now ask your system at any time exactly what a bulk run wrote and what is recoverable, and a short list of routine, read-only checks no longer interrupts you for permission every time (anything that writes anywhere still always asks first). Finally, a privacy-safe, saved summary of each bulk run — with no raw personal data in it — now proves what happened and that you approved it, and a run's outcome is always described from exactly what happened, never rounded up to "done" if it wasn't. No breaking changes: everything your system could already do continues to work exactly as before, and every previously released version still installs and runs correctly.
bundles.recommendation_reason: If you run bulk write-back batches, build or rebuild capabilities, or want a durable, privacy-safe record of what a run did, this update makes each of those safer and more honest — most operators should take it.

bundles.changelog: Your system now prevents capability code from reaching the bulk-write engine's internal parts directly — it must go through the approved interface — and upgrades now detect a wider range of pre-existing custom code that needs migrating to stay safe.
bundles.recommendation_reason: If your system has any capabilities that write in bulk, or you plan to add or rebuild one, this closes an internal path a capability could otherwise use to bypass the approved way of reaching the bulk-write engine, and it makes an upgrade more thorough about recognizing your own older custom code that needs to come along safely — most operators should take it.

bundles.changelog: Your system now checks each capability's health at the start of every session and tells you plainly if one is switched off or a bulk job was interrupted — it will not say everything is running normally when it isn't. Turning on a capability you have built or rebuilt is now a single short command instead of a long one that could break when pasted.
bundles.recommendation_reason: If your system has (or will have) a capability that writes in bulk, this makes the start-of-session status honest about anything switched off or interrupted, and turns switching a capability on into a single reliable step — most operators should take it.

bundles.changelog: This update makes building and turning on capabilities more reliable. Turning a capability on now always gives you an exact, ready-to-paste next step when it can't work out the details on its own — it never asks you to fix a command yourself. When a capability's code needs a third-party software package, the system now installs and records it for you automatically, so you never run an install command or edit a requirements file by hand. It also refuses to silently reuse a set-aside capability whose code has changed until it has been reconciled, and tells you plainly if the same capability was accidentally recorded twice.
bundles.recommendation_reason: This is a reliability fix for building and operating capabilities — safer turn-on with an always-paste-ready next step, automatic third-party dependency handling, and clearer honesty about set-aside or duplicated capabilities. It adds no breaking changes and touches none of your data, so most operators should take it.

bundles.changelog: This update closes a safety gap in turning capabilities on. Before, a capability could be marked ready even while a hand-rolled file still wrote to your external world by a path that skipped the safe, gated write surface. Now turning a capability on refuses to go live while any such bypass is open, and it names the exact file to rebuild. Whenever a bypass like that exists, the health check and the completion check report the whole project as not-normal / not-done and point you to the file — and they fail safe rather than ever reporting a false all-clear. Once you rebuild the flagged file through the safe path, the block clears on its own the next time the check runs. No breaking changes, and none of your data is touched.
bundles.recommendation_reason: This is a reliability fix that closes a false all-clear when turning capabilities on: a capability can no longer be marked ready around a hand-rolled writer that bypasses the safe, gated write surface, and the system now tells you the exact file to rebuild and fails safe instead of reporting a false all-clear. It adds no breaking changes and touches none of your data, so most operators should take it.

bundles.changelog: This update fixes the one situation that could leave your project stuck with no way forward. A capability that needs to LOOK at your outside system before proposing changes can now do that through a safe, read-only path -- previously there was no legitimate way to do it, so such a capability could neither be rebuilt nor switched on, and that held the whole project back. Files that are not part of your live setup, such as the tests that come with a capability, no longer block anything, though they are still listed for you. And if a flagged file genuinely cannot be rebuilt automatically -- because it also does something else you rely on, like sending your daily email -- the system now says so plainly and lets you record that you accept the risk of leaving it as it is, instead of asking you to rebuild something that cannot be rebuilt. That decision is kept on file, stays visible, and is asked again the moment the file changes. Anything that genuinely still needs fixing continues to block, exactly as before.
bundles.recommendation_reason: This is a reliability fix that removes a dead end: a capability that must read your outside system before proposing changes had no safe way to do so, which could leave the whole project unable to switch anything on. It also stops files that are not part of your live setup from blocking you, and gives you an honest, recorded way to accept a file that cannot be rebuilt automatically. Everything that genuinely needs attention still blocks.

bundles.changelog: When a capability of yours cannot yet look at your outside system in a safe, read-only way, the message you get now names the exact adapter that needs a read-only reader added to it, and says plainly that rebuilding the capability will not fix this -- instead of sending you in a circle trying to rebuild the capability itself. The health check and turning a capability on also now describe each blocking item honestly: a file that genuinely needs to be rebuilt still gets that guidance, but something else recorded on the same list -- for example, a safety check that itself could not finish -- is described in its own words instead of being told, wrongly, to rebuild something that was never the problem. This release also makes sure every upgrade and safety review actually checks and records whether each capability can look at your outside system safely, closing a gap where that check could silently be skipped without anyone knowing. It also fixes a self-check your system runs when you build or rebuild a capability, to prove that capability's own tests would really catch a mistake: on Python 3.12, if those tests were not written in the required style, you got only a generic "your tests do not pass cleanly" message, instead of the actionable guidance telling you to write them as the required kind of test. You now always get the actionable guidance, on every Python version this wizard supports.
bundles.recommendation_reason: This is a reliability fix for a misleading error message that sent you in a circle: when a capability could not yet look at your outside system safely, it told you to rebuild the capability instead of naming the adapter that actually needed the fix. It also closes a gap in the update tool itself, so the safety check behind every upgrade actually runs and is recorded rather than silently being skippable, and fixes a self-check on a capability's own tests so it always gives you actionable guidance on the Python version this wizard has you install. No breaking changes; most operators should take it.

bundles.changelog: Your capabilities' safe, read-only access to your outside system is now found by what a file declares it provides, rather than by what the file is named. Before this, that lookup expected an exact naming pattern, so a project whose files were set up before that pattern existed could fail here even though everything it needed was already in place -- and the failure was silent about why. It now works correctly for that kind of project too. If a capability's read-only file exists but what it declares cannot be read -- for example, a registration written inside a function instead of at the top level of the file -- the message you get now names that exact file, instead of the generic message telling you the capability itself needs to be rebuilt. The notices an upgrade produces are more accurate and more specific too. The status notice now tells a test file apart from a file your system actually runs: a test file is told plainly that nothing running uses it and there is nothing for you to do, rather than being told, wrongly, that its outside access was switched off and that it needs to be rebuilt. That notice, and the summary printed when an upgrade finishes, now show each flagged file's full location, not just its name, so two files that happen to share a name in different folders are no longer shown as if they were the same file. When an upgrade cannot read what a file has registered, it now says so plainly and names that file, instead of quietly pointing at a different, unrelated file as the cause, and it is written into your pending-work list as its own item. And after you record a decision to leave a flagged file exactly as it is, the notice now says plainly that this did not switch anything back on -- it only means that file stops holding up the rest of your system.
bundles.recommendation_reason: This is a reliability fix for a lookup that could come up empty and stay silent about it: the safe, read-only access a capability needs is now found by what a file declares it provides rather than by what the file is named, so a project whose files were set up before that naming convention existed now works. It also makes an upgrade's notices honest about which file they mean -- naming the exact file when a declaration cannot be read, showing each flagged file's full location, telling a test file apart from a file your system actually runs, and never blaming an unrelated file. No breaking changes; most operators should take it.

bundles.changelog: You can now run a single trial of one operation, and that trial produces the proof that switching a capability on has always required. Until now nothing you could run produced that proof, so a capability could be set up correctly and still never become switchable. A trial is a real change to your real system, made and then put straight back. Here is what a trial does. It refuses up front anything it cannot establish from what that operation's own adapter declares about itself -- silence is a refusal, never a pass. It requires your approval on the command. For an operation your system gates -- one classed as impossible to undo, as running unattended on a schedule, or as touching sensitive data, and any operation carrying no risk contract at all, which is treated as the most protected of those -- a trial requires a limit on how much that operation may touch, refuses to run without one, and counts what it uses against it; that count covers this one approved trial and is not a lifetime running total. That does not cover every operation. In particular, one whose contract classes its changes as reversible, and which does not separately require an approved phase, is not gated here, and a trial of it enforces no limit at all. Reversible is what that setting defaults to, so it is worth knowing which classification an operation carries before leaning on a trial's limit. What it is about to do is written and flushed to disk before the change is attempted: once that record exists, an interruption at any later instant leaves a durable record that can be found again, and before it exists an interruption leaves nothing changed and no record -- nothing was changed, and there is nothing to find. And it writes the proof only if it observed the whole round trip -- the change landing, and the state coming back -- and writes nothing at all otherwise. A trial passing tells you this operation can be made and put back. It does not tell you that a later live run will be permitted. Alongside that, every state that holds something up now names, in one place, the exact instruction and command that clears it, or is written down in plain language as needing no action; a state that is in neither list now fails the build instead of shipping silently, and a unit left needing recovery can be cleared once the system has looked at the state it was actually left in. Acknowledging a risk is now limited to an explicit list of the states that qualify, so a state added later cannot become acknowledgeable just by not being excluded. You can now mark a recorded acceptance repudiated, which switches that capability back off and queues it for a fresh trial rather than leaving live permission standing behind a record you no longer trust. A paused wrapper now records the moment its guard stops a scheduled run, so a job that has quietly stopped producing output becomes visible. And two new build-time checks were added: one flags a file that hard-codes your own confirmation instead of asking you, and one flags a repair instruction hand-written into the surface that displays it rather than coming from the single place those instructions are defined. ONE BEHAVIOUR DELIBERATELY CHANGED, AND IT CAN RE-BLOCK SOMETHING YOU HAD ALREADY CLEARED: a recorded risk-acceptance is now honoured only for a file that genuinely cannot be rebuilt automatically. Before this version such a record was honoured for any flagged file, including one the rebuild flow could have fixed, so recording the acceptance took that file off the blocked list and its rebuild never had to happen -- that was the defect. After this upgrade a record of that second kind stops counting: the file it names goes back to being blocked and shown as needing a rebuild, and nothing tells you that a record you made has become inert. Records against files that genuinely need a person are unaffected. Three things are stated as declared rather than proven, on purpose: whether an adapter's undo is safe to repeat is a declaration the system reads and cannot verify; recovery may issue a write that changes nothing, because restoring a value to what it already is remains a real call to the outside service; and the upgrade step that adds the new undo declaration to an adapter you or your assistant wrote sets it to the safe value, never to yes -- only a person, or an assistant that has read the code, may change it. Four situations remain open and are named rather than implied fixed: if the outside system a capability writes to is named differently from the capability's own name, that capability can be switched on and still have every live write refused, because the check that decides whether your approval covers an operation compares the capability's own name against the name of the outside system, and there is nothing you can do to that capability to make them match; a retrial item's next step exists on disk and in the skills but is not printed by any surface; a paused hand-rolled writer's pair of marker files has a written route out but no single command that performs it; and a wrapper's guard is recognised by what it looks like, which does not establish that it will fire. Upgrading in one step works from v0.6.9 and later; a system still on v0.3.0 through v0.6.8 must be brought to v0.6.9 or later first.
bundles.recommendation_reason: This release closes two situations you could get into and not get out of. A capability that was set up correctly could never be switched on, because the proof acceptance requires had no producer you could run; there is now a trial command that produces it. And every state that holds something up now names its own way out in one place. It also gives you a sanctioned way to repudiate an acceptance record you no longer trust, which switches the capability back off rather than leaving permission standing, and makes a scheduled job that has quietly stopped producing output visible. Read the two cautions in the change notes before applying: a risk-acceptance you recorded against a file that CAN be rebuilt automatically stops counting after this upgrade, so that file becomes blocked again with no notice that your record went inert; and a capability whose outside system is named differently from the capability itself can still be switched on and have every live write refused -- that one is named, not fixed. Most operators should take it.
